claims.claim: Joseph is 17 at Gen 37:2, "the son of his old age", and loved by Jacob "more than all his children".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 37:2–3, read in full via BibleGateway.

claims.claim: The *ketonet passim* is a long-sleeved tunic reaching wrists and ankles — a garment of status, not manual labour.
claims.evidence: BDB H3801 (*kĕtōnet*, "tunic") + H6446 (*pas*, "of the tunic reaching to palms and soles"); Skinner, ICC pp. 442–449 (sleeved tunic to wrists/ankles, cf. 2 Sam 13:18); JFB Gen 37 (reaching to hands and feet, worn by persons not much occupied with manual labour).

claims.claim: "Coat of many colours" is a mistranslation carried from the LXX's *chitōn poikilos*; "variegated/varicolored tunic" is closer to the Hebrew.
claims.evidence: NETS Gen 37:31–32 "variegated tunic"; NASB "varicolored tunic" (BibleHub); Skinner pp. 442–449. The KJV follows the LXX/Vulgate tradition.

claims.claim: Joseph dreams twice: sheaves bowing (an agricultural scene) and sun, moon, and eleven stars bowing.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 37:5–11, read in full.

claims.claim: Rachel was already dead when the second dream was told, so the "moon" cannot literally be Rachel; interpreters differ (Leah vs the household).
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining "Joseph" (Rachel died in childbirth, Gen 35:16–18; interpreters differ on the moon); Josephus, Ant. II.2, treats Rachel as alive at the second dream — recorded as a divergence (see clm-jo-085).

claims.claim: The brothers' hatred is driven by the coat, the dreams, and Joseph's evil report of them (37:2); they "could not speak peaceably unto him" (37:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 37:2–4, read in full; BDB H7965 *šālôm* sense 3, "speak peace" Gen 37:4 (JE).

claims.claim: Dothan lies ~13–15 miles north of Shechem.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining (~13 miles farther north); Skinner p. 442–449 (Tell Dothan, ~15 mi N of Shechem). The two read figures differ slightly; both are recorded.

claims.claim: The sale narrative is a double recension: J has the brothers sell Joseph to Ishmaelites on Judah's advice (tunic-motive primary); E has Midianites kidnap him while Reuben plans to rescue him (dream-motive primary).
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 442–449 — recorded as Skinner's critical analysis, not as the text's own presentation.

claims.claim: The price of twenty pieces of silver is consistent with an early-second-millennium slave price, rising in later centuries.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, citing Kitchen (*On the Reliability of the OT*) — **second-hand** (Kitchen not read directly).

claims.claim: The caravan travelled the Gilead–Beisan–Ramleh–Egypt route carrying balm, myrrh, and spicery for embalming.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 442–449 — Skinner's reconstruction of the route and the cargo's Egyptian use.

claims.claim: Joseph's dreams are prophetic dreams — "the lowest grade of prophecy".
claims.evidence: BDB H2472 *ḥălôm* sense 2, citing Joseph Gen 37:5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 19, 20 and Num 12:6 ("of a lower order of prophets than Moses").

claims.claim: The tunic is stripped (37:23) and dipped in a goat's blood (37:31): Joseph's fortunes rise and fall with his clothing.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 37:23, 31–32, read in full; Bible Odyssey, "Joseph and His Clothing" (episodes "held together by Joseph being given or losing garments").

claims.claim: Genesis 38 (Judah and Tamar) is integral to the Joseph cycle, not an interpolation: Judah's Canaanite alliance endangered the call, and the migration to Egypt is in part its protection.
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 37 intro + Gen 38 (integral; "Judah's Canaanite alliance endangered the call"); Skinner, ICC pp. 449–456, treats ch. 38 as tribal-history substratum — "legend independent of Joseph cycle" — while also giving its clan origins (Er/Onan extinction; Perez/Zerah rivalry, Perez supremacy, David ancestry, Ruth 4:18–22). The two positions are preserved as a disagreement.

claims.claim: The levirate custom has origins probably in Chaldea and is found among Indians, Persians, and other Asian and African nations.
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 38 — K&D's comparative claim; not independently verified against those cultures this session.

claims.claim: Judah's sentence on Tamar (burning) is harsher than Mosaic law (stoning for the affianced, Deut 22:20–21, 23–24; burning only in Lev 21:9 and 20:14).
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 38 — recorded as K&D's legal comparison of the pre-Mosaic sentence with the Mosaic code.

claims.claim: Tamar's motive was children, not lust; Judah confesses, "She is more righteous than I."
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 38:26, read in full; K&D, Gen 38 (Tamar's motive children not lust — Theodoret, **second-hand** via K&D).

claims.claim: Potiphar is Eg. Pedephre, "He whom the sun-god gives", chief of the cooks/butchers (śar haṭṭabbāḥîm); the LXX calls him "Pharao's gelding, a chief butcher".
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 456–460 (Pedephre); NETS Gen 37:36 ("Petephres, Pharao's gelding, a chief butcher").

claims.claim: Potiphar is presented as a eunuch who is also married — a tension in the narrative.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 456–460 (notes the eunuch-marriage problem); Jubilees 39–40, Josephus Ant. II.4, and Philo, *De Josepho* §27, all call Potiphar a eunuch — the tradition preserves rather than resolves the tension.

claims.claim: "The LORD was with Joseph" is the refrain of ch. 39 (vv. 2–3, 21, 23) and of the prison (39:21, 23).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 39:2–3, 21, 23, read in full; BiblicalTraining notes the same refrain.

claims.claim: Joseph refuses Potiphar's wife on grounds of trust in his master and sin against God (39:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 39:9, read in full. Philo's elaboration of Hebrew marriage customs (*De Josepho* §§42–48) is Philo's own, not the text's.

claims.claim: The Tale of Two Brothers parallels Gen 39 only in the seduction and false-accusation episode; the rest of the tale (gods, transformations, self-mutilation) diverges completely.
claims.evidence: Tale of Two Brothers, Moldenke 1898 tr., read in full (Papyrus d'Orbiney); BiblicalTraining ("parallel 'limited to that episode,' rest fantastic"); Bible Odyssey, "Joseph and His Clothing" (Matthews & Benjamin, *Old Testament Parallels*, 65–69 — **second-hand** via Bible Odyssey).

claims.claim: The Tale of Two Brothers dates to the 19th Dynasty, c. 1225 BC (Papyrus d'Orbiney, British Museum).
claims.evidence: Moldenke 1898 tr. (Papyrus d'Orbiney); the Hollis-based PDF quoted in search results dates the papyrus to 1225 BCE, 19th Dynasty (**second-hand** via search results — see §12.4; the papyrus's identity rests on Moldenke, read in full; only the date is second-hand).

claims.claim: The imprisonment is indispensable in J and embarrassing in E — a source-critical divergence.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 456–460 — recorded as Skinner's analysis.

claims.claim: The cupbearer and baker dream on the same night; Joseph asks, "Do not interpretations belong to God?" (40:8); the cupbearer is restored in three days, the baker hanged.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 40, read in full.

claims.claim: The cupbearer forgets Joseph for two full years (40:23; 41:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 40:23; 41:1, read in full. Philo, *De Josepho* §§80–124, reads the forgetting as providence — "that the prosperity of the young man should not be owing to man, but rather to [God] himself" — recorded as Philo's reading.

claims.claim: Pharaoh dreams twice in one night: seven fat and seven lean kine coming up out of the river, and seven full and seven thin ears; the doubling means the thing is established by God (41:32).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 41:1–7, 25–32, read in full.

claims.claim: The narrative uses Egyptian loanwords and titles: *ʾāḥû* (Nile-grass), *ḥarṭummîm* (from *ḥereṭ*, stylus — the *hierogrammateis*), *ʾabrēk* (uncertain; Coptic *abork*), Zaphnath-paaneah (Coptic proposals), Potiphera ("he who is of the sun"), On = Heliopolis ("house of the sun", temple with the learned priesthood first among Egypt's priest colleges, Herod. 2.3).
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 41 — recorded as K&D's analysis (citing Hengstenberg for Egyptian customs and Pliny *h.n.* xix.1 for byssus — both **second-hand** via K&D). *ʾabrēk* is explicitly uncertain in K&D and in BiblicalTraining.

claims.claim: Joseph shaved before appearing before Pharaoh, per Egyptian custom.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 41:14, read in full; K&D, Gen 41 (Hengstenberg p. 30 — **second-hand** via K&D); BiblicalTraining.

claims.claim: Joseph is 30 at his rise (41:46) — thirteen years after the sale at 17.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 37:2; 41:46, read in full; arithmetic; BiblicalTraining (Joseph 17 at Gen 37:2, 30 at Gen 41:46).

claims.claim: The meaning of Zaphnath-paaneah is debated: "salvation of the world" or "sustainer of life" (K&D, Coptic) vs "revealer of secrets" (Josephus) vs "the god speaks and he lives" (BiblicalTraining).
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 41; Josephus, Ant. II.6 ("Psothom Phanech = the revealer of secrets"); BiblicalTraining ("several proposals incl. 'the god speaks and he lives,' meaning still debated").

claims.claim: Asenath is the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis); her name is possibly connected with the goddess Neith.
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 41 (Asenath possibly connected with Neith; Potiphera = "he who is of the sun"); BiblicalTraining (Asenath "belonging to [the goddess] Neith").

claims.claim: Manasseh means "God made me forget [all my toil]"; Ephraim, "God made me fruitful in the land of my affliction" (41:51–52).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 41:51–52, read in full.

claims.claim: A fifth part was stored in the years of plenty (41:34); state granaries were a standing feature of Egyptian administration, and the "superintendent of the granaries" was a high officer distinct from the vizier.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 41:34–36, read in full; Skinner, ICC pp. 463–473 (citing Erman for the granaries and the office — Erman **second-hand** via Skinner).

claims.claim: Egyptian famine relief is attested in the sources Skinner cites: Ameny of Beni-Hasan (12th Dynasty, Usertsen I) and an El-Kab inscription of the 17th Dynasty ("When a famine arose, lasting many years, I distributed corn").
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 463–473, citing Erman — **second-hand** (Erman not read directly).

claims.claim: Yanhamu, a Semitic minister of Amenhotep IV and governor of Yarimutu in the Amarna letters, controlled state granaries and sold grain to foreigners; identifying him with Joseph is "too slender", and Marquart's suggestion that the Joseph portrait draws on Yanhamu is only "conceivable", with points of contact restricted.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 501–502 (Yanhamu; Knudtzon, *El-Amarna Tafeln*, p. 407 — **second-hand** via Skinner — for the people parting with sons/daughters and house woodwork for corn).

claims.claim: The Arisu/Irsu parallel (Papyrus Harris, end of the 19th Dynasty) "vanishes on closer inspection".
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 501–502 — recorded as Skinner's judgment.

claims.claim: Winckler's Musri-theory is rejected.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 463–473 — Skinner's rejection; Winckler not read directly.

claims.claim: A seven-year famine is "at home in Egyptian tradition": the Famine Stela at Sehel (Ptolemaic) tells of a seven-year famine under Djoser.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Joseph" — **second-hand** (the Famine Stela not read directly).

claims.claim: Joseph's agrarian policy (47:13–26) proceeds in sequence — money, then livestock, then land, then persons surrendered; the priests' land is exempt; the fifth part becomes a permanent statute "to this day".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 47:13–26, read in full; NETS Gen 47:20–26 (same sequence; v. 25 "You have saved us… we will be slaves to Pharao").

claims.claim: Gen 47:21 is a textual variant: MT "moved the people into the cities" vs SP/LXX "reduced the people to servitude".
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining (MT vs SP/LXX variant; several modern translations follow SP/LXX — the SP reading is **second-hand** via BiblicalTraining); NETS Gen 47:21 ("the people he subjugated to him as slaves") — the LXX reading, confirmed by direct read.

claims.claim: How far the narrator means to commend Joseph's agrarian policy is ambiguous.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining ("commentators differ over how far the narrator means to commend it"); Skinner, ICC pp. 498–501 (the interest is aetiological; Erman — **second-hand** via Skinner: the system arose after the Hyksos expulsion and the founding of the New Empire, when the old landed aristocracy was exterminated; uncertain whether Egyptian tradition or Israelite imagination).

claims.claim: Joseph is the lexicon's own example of administrative wisdom: BDB cites Gen 41:33, 39 under *ḥākām*, "wise in the administration of affairs".
claims.evidence: BDB H2450 *ḥākām* sense 2 ("Joseph in Egypt Genesis 41:33, 39 (E)").

claims.claim: Joseph stored all the silver and gold in the king's treasury, "not appropriating a single drachm".
claims.evidence: Philo, *De Josepho* §XLIV — Philo's elaboration; not stated in Genesis.

claims.claim: During the seven famine years the Nile did not overflow and irrigated only a few places on the banks of the river.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 45 — Jubilees' detail; Genesis does not state it.

claims.claim: The brothers make two journeys with four interviews; ch. 42 is mainly E, chs. 43–44 mainly J.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 473–490 — recorded as Skinner's source analysis.

claims.claim: Joseph tests his brothers: the spy accusation, three days in prison, Simeon bound as hostage, and the silver returned in their sacks.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 42, read in full.

claims.claim: The brothers confess divine punishment and recall Joseph's pleading (42:21): "we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 42:21–22, read in full.

claims.claim: Reuben's pledge (his two sons as surety) is rejected; Judah's surety (43:9, "let me bear the blame… for ever") is accepted.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 42:37; 43:8–10, read in full.

claims.claim: Egyptians may not eat with Hebrews (43:32), and shepherds are detestable to Egyptians (46:34).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 43:32; 46:34, read in full.

claims.claim: Benjamin's portion is five times the others' in the MT (43:34); Josephus says double, Jubilees says seven times.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 43:34 (5×), read in full; Josephus, Ant. II.6 (Benjamin's mess DOUBLE); Jubilees 42 (Benjamin's portion SEVEN times larger). The MT reading is established; the divergence is a tradition question, not a textual one.

claims.claim: The silver cup is hidden in Benjamin's sack and Joseph claims divination by it (44:5, 15); Josephus has a golden cup, and Jubilees reframes the divination as delight in the cup.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 44:2, 5, 15 (silver cup; divination), read in full; Josephus, Ant. II.6 (GOLDEN cup); Jubilees 43 ("a man delighteth in his cup").

claims.claim: Judah's speech (44:18–34) offers himself as slave in Benjamin's stead; the man who once proposed selling a brother into slavery now offers himself instead.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 44:18–34, read in full; BiblicalTraining ("the man who had once proposed selling a brother into slavery now offered himself instead").

claims.claim: Joseph reveals himself with the theology of providence: "God did send me before you to preserve life" (45:5–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 45:5–8, read in full.

claims.claim: Seventy souls descend to Egypt (46:27 MT); the LXX and Acts 7:14 give seventy-five, following the LXX's additional descendants of Joseph.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 46:27 (70), read in full; NETS Gen 46 ("who came into Egypt were seventy-five"); BiblicalTraining (Acts 7:14 figure of 75 follows LXX).

claims.claim: Joseph's forgiveness is unconditional and unchanging after the reconciliation.
claims.evidence: Philo, *De Josepho* §XLIV ("I do not change my disposition with the changes of time, nor, after I have agreed to a reconciliation and forgiveness, will I ever do anything inconsistent") — Philo's reading.

claims.claim: The Beersheba theophany (46:2–4) is the only theophany in Gen 37–50, and no theophany is given to Joseph himself.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 46:2–4, read in full; K&D, Gen 37 intro ("only one theophany in the whole section (Beersheba, Gen 46:2–4)"). Skinner's "no theophanies" (p. 437) refers to Joseph's own story; the two are reconciled on this reading.

claims.claim: Jacob is 130 at his arrival in Egypt (47:9), lives 17 years there, and dies at 147 (47:28).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 47:9, 28, read in full.

claims.claim: Goshen is the eastern Nile Delta, often identified with the Wadi Tumilat; "the land of Rameses" (47:11) is taken by many as an updating to a later place name.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining ("Goshen = eastern Nile Delta, often Wadi Tumilat"; "'land of Rameses' (47:11) taken by many as updating to a later place name"). The updating is an inference, labelled as such.

claims.claim: Jacob adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as equals of Reuben and Simeon (48:5) and crosses his hands, the right on Ephraim the younger.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 48:5, 13–20, read in full. Skinner's "crossing of hands guided by supernatural impulse" (pp. 502–507) is Skinner's reading, not the text's.

claims.claim: The younger-son motif continues: Ephraim is set before Manasseh (48:19).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 48:19, read in full; Bible Odyssey, "Sibling Rivalries and Younger Sons" (Gen 48:19 continues the cycle).

claims.claim: Genesis 49 is "one of the oldest pieces of Hebrew poetry": a series of oracles on the twelve tribes as unfolded in Judges and the early monarchy, *vaticinia ex eventu*, the horizon closing at David/Solomon, the Judah oracle presupposing the Davidic kingdom, the final shape by a Judahite poet of the David/Solomon age, incorporated by J.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 507–540 — Skinner's critical dating. Directly contradicted by clm-jo-062 (K&D); preserved as a disagreement.

claims.claim: The *vaticinia ex eventu* reading of Gen 49 is rejected: attacks on its genuineness proceed from an a priori denial of supernatural prophecy, and *ʾaḥărît hayyāmîm* means "the end of the days" — the Messianic age of consummation, not merely some future time.
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 49 (citing Hengstenberg's *Christology* i, p. 76 — **second-hand** via K&D). Directly contradicts clm-jo-061 (Skinner); preserved as a disagreement.

claims.claim: Reuben forfeits the firstborn rank: leadership passes to Judah and the double portion to Joseph (1 Chr 5:1–2).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 49:3–4, read in full; K&D, Gen 49 (1 Chron 5:1–2).

claims.claim: Simeon and Levi: *mekērôt* is a hapax legomenon (weapons/swords); "I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel" is fulfilled in Simeon's weakness (Num 26:14), Simeon's omission in Deut 33, Simeon's cities within Judah (Josh 19:1–9), and Levi's priesthood.
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 49 — K&D's fulfilment reading. K&D treat the transformation of Levi's curse into blessing — which Jacob's address does not intimate — as proof of the blessing's genuineness.

claims.claim: Shiloh (49:10) is read three ways: (a) the Messiah's personal name, "the man, or bearer, of rest" (K&D; Calvin, "He who is to be sent"; b. Sanh. 98b, R. Shela); (b) the place Shiloh, "until he [Judah] come to Shiloh" (Herder, Ewald) — rejected by Skinner, K&D, and Calvin as unhistorical; (c) the LXX, "until the things stored up for him come" (NETS).
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 49 (Shiloh as personal name; *ʿad kî* not exclusive; Ezek 21:27 confirms the personal reading); Calvin on Gen 49 (place reading "entirely destitute of reason"); JFB Gen 49 (Shiloh = "the sent", "the seed", "the peaceable one" — the Messiah); Skinner, ICC pp. 521–524 (personal-name reading from Münster 1534, now "universally abandoned" among critics; place reading unhistorical); NETS Gen 49:10. (b. Sanh. 98b is **second-hand** via Skinner; Herder and Ewald are **second-hand** via Skinner/K&D; none read directly.)

claims.claim: "The gathering of the peoples" (49:10) means the willing obedience of the nations (*ʿammîm*, plural = Gentiles); the LXX agrees in sense ("he is the expectation of nations").
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 49 (*yiqqahat ʿammîm* = willing obedience of the nations); Calvin on Gen 49 (*ʿammîm* plural = Gentiles); NETS Gen 49:10 ("he is the expectation of nations").

claims.claim: Jacob is buried at Machpelah; the embalming takes forty days and the mourning seventy days (50:3).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 50:1–13, read in full (Egyptian embalming custom; cf. §4).

claims.claim: Joseph dies at 110 — "Egyptian texts repeatedly present 110 years as the ideal length of life"; Joshua dies at the same age (Josh 24:29).
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining — **second-hand** (the Egyptian ideal-age claim not independently verified against Egyptian texts this session).

claims.claim: "Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to save much people alive" (50:20).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 50:20, read in full; NETS Gen 50:20 ("God deliberated concerning me for good things in order that a numerous people might be sustained").

claims.claim: Joseph's bones: the oath is kept (Exod 13:19; Josh 24:32; Heb 11:22).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 50:24–25, read in full; BiblicalTraining (Exod 13:19; Josh 24:32; Heb 11:22).

claims.claim: Joseph's Tomb near Nablus/Shechem has "long [been] venerated" but its identification "cannot be confirmed".
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining — the identification is unsettled on the evidence read.

claims.claim: "House of Joseph" is used for the northern kingdom (Amos 5:6, 15; 6:6; Ezek 37:15–19; Obad 18; Zech 10:6; Ps 78:67 — God "refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose… Judah/Zion").
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining's survey of the usage (Amos 5:6, 15; 6:6; Ezek 37:15–19; Obad 18; Zech 10:6; Ps 77:15; 80:1; 81:5; 78:67; Rev 7:8).

claims.claim: Joseph-Christ typology: the NT never explicitly calls Joseph a type; the early church drew correspondences (beloved son, rejected, sold for silver, lowly then exalted, source of life for wrongdoers); some limit typology to NT-identified persons, while Stephen's speech (Acts 7) is cited for a wider reading.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining (NT never explicitly calls Joseph a type; early church correspondences; Acts 7 cited for the wider reading). A theological judgment, not a textual claim.

claims.claim: No pharaoh is named; dating depends on the exodus chronology. The early-exodus reckoning (1 Kgs 6:1, 480 years; Exod 12:40, 430 years) puts the exodus in the mid-15th century BC, Jacob's arrival in the 19th century BC, and Joseph under the 12th Dynasty (Middle Kingdom). The late-exodus reckoning puts Joseph in the Second Intermediate Period under the Hyksos (c. 1650–1550 BC), capital Avaris in the eastern Delta near Goshen. "A Semitic official would have risen most easily under such rulers, although Egyptian records show that Asiatics could hold high office at other periods as well. The question remains open."
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining — both options preserved as a disagreement; the dossier takes no position.

claims.claim: No direct Egyptian attestation for Joseph exists, and no Egyptian record names him; this absence does not by itself disprove the narrative, and no identification (Yanhamu, Arisu/Irsu, a Hyksos vizier) is established.
claims.evidence: Methodological claim grounded in the read sources: BiblicalTraining (no pharaoh named; the question remains open); Skinner, ICC pp. 501–502 (Yanhamu "too slender"; Arisu/Irsu "vanishes on closer inspection"). See §7.3.

claims.claim: Semitic/Asiatic presence in Egypt in the early second millennium is attested: the Beni Hasan 19th-century BC tomb painting of Asiatics in multicoloured garments; Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446 (18th century BC) listing household servants, several with Northwest Semitic names; Tell el-Dabʿa (Avaris) with a large Asiatic population in the eastern Delta.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining — **second-hand** (Beni Hasan, Brooklyn 35.1446, and Tell el-Dabʿa not independently read this session).

claims.claim: The Joseph story is the "finest example… of 'novelistic' narrative" in the Old Testament, with the ruling idea of 50:20 and providence immanent throughout.
claims.evidence: Skinner, ICC pp. 437–442 — recorded as Skinner's literary judgment.

claims.claim: The divine names shift across the section: Jehovah is absent in Gen 37, occurs 9× in Gen 38–39, then disappears after ch. 40 except 49:18; Elohim occurs 18× and Ha-Elohim 7× in chs. 40–50.
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 37 intro — recorded as K&D's count.

claims.claim: Joseph is not a medium of salvation like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; the Joseph-as-type-of-Christ reading is not represented by prophets, Christ, or apostles the way Exodus guidance is (Hos 11:1/Matt 2:15).
claims.evidence: K&D, Gen 37 intro — K&D's theological judgment; preserved as a disagreement with the wider typological reading (clm-jo-073).

claims.claim: The Tale of Sinuhe parallels Joseph structurally: shaving and new garments on reintegration, the exile-and-return arc, an Asiatic's rise at a foreign court and royal favour, and "dream" language in Sinuhe's reply.
claims.evidence: Tale of Sinuhe, Gardiner 1916 tr., read in full — parallel, not dependence; no claim of derivation is made.

claims.claim: Sinuhe differs from Joseph decisively: Sinuhe is an Egyptian fleeing Egypt who longs to return; Joseph is a Hebrew brought to Egypt against his will who stays; Sinuhe is first-person autobiography, Joseph third-person narrative; Sinuhe has no dreams, no famine administration, and no reconciliation of brothers.
claims.evidence: Tale of Sinuhe, Gardiner 1916 tr., read in full, compared with KJV Gen 37–50, read in full.

claims.claim: Jubilees ties Yom Kippur to Joseph's sale: the coat is sent on the tenth of the seventh month, Jacob mourns Joseph one year, and "three mournings upon Israel in one month" (Bilhah and Dinah die too); Israel is ordained to afflict themselves on the 10th of the 7th month with a young goat, once a year, "for they had grieved the affection of their father regarding Joseph his son."
claims.evidence: Jubilees 34 — Jubilees' own aetiology; not in Genesis.

claims.claim: In Jubilees, Potiphar is eunuch, chief cook, AND priest of Heliopolis — the same person as Potiphera, whose daughter Asenath Joseph marries.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 39–40 — Jubilees' harmonisation; Genesis distinguishes Potiphar (37:36; 39:1) from Potiphera (41:45).

claims.claim: Philo reads Joseph as the statesman (*bios politikos*): shepherding is the prelude to kingship, household management is "a city on a small and contracted scale", and the coat of many colours figures the multiform political constitution.
claims.evidence: Philo, *De Josepho* §§1–13, 28–38 — Philo's allegorical reading.

claims.claim: Josephus's retelling diverges from Genesis at: Potiphar as chief cook (not captain of the guard); Rachel alive at the second dream; the golden (not silver) cup; Benjamin's portion double (not fivefold); Joseph restoring the land to its owners (vs the MT's tenure change); Heliopolis (not Goshen) as the settlement.
claims.evidence: Josephus, Ant. II.2–8 (Whiston tr.), read in full — recorded as Josephus's retelling, not as the biblical text.

claims.claim: The theology of 50:20 is providence immanent: God intends good from human evil, and the wrong is not excused — the brothers' guilt is named throughout.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 45:5–8; 50:19–20, read in full; Skinner, ICC p. 437 (ruling idea 50:20); BiblicalTraining ("wrong not excused (brothers' guilt named throughout)").

connections.note: Joseph's birth — bridge from the Isaac, Jacob, and Esau category (narrativeOrder 13).
Rachel's death in childbirth — bears on the second dream's "moon".
"In thee shall all families of the earth be blessed" — the blessing the Joseph story carries to the nations.
The 400-year affliction prophecy — the descent to Egypt begins its fulfilment.
Twenty shekels, the valuation of a male aged 5–20 — the slave-price parallel for Gen 37:28 (Skinner).
Thirty shekels for a slave gored by an ox — the contrasting price parallel (Skinner).
The Aaronic benediction — the threefold invocation of Deity paralleling Gen 48:15–16 (Skinner).
Dreams as the lower order of prophecy, below Moses — BDB's frame for ḥălôm.
Simeon's census (22,200) — the fulfilment of "I will divide them… and scatter them" (K&D on Gen 49:7).
The Blessing of Moses on Joseph — the later, dependent blessing (Skinner: Deut 33 is later than and dependent on Gen 49).
Simeon's cities within Judah's inheritance — the fulfilment of the scattering (K&D).
Joshua dies at 110 (the ideal age) and Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem. The connection object spans Josh 24:29–32; the exact verses are Josh 24:29 and 24:32.
"The house of Joseph" takes Bethel — the tribal usage. The connection object spans Judg 1:22–35; the exact verses are Judg 1:22–23 and 1:35.
Midianites called "Ishmaelites" — the terms overlap, bearing on the J/E double recension (BiblicalTraining).
Perez → David — the genealogy that makes Gen 38's Perez supremacy matter (Skinner).
Tamar's ketonet passim — the same phrase as Joseph's coat, marking a king's virgin daughter.
The birthright passes to Joseph's sons and leadership to Judah — the fulfilment of Gen 49:3–4, 8–10 (K&D).

"The sons of Jacob and Joseph" (77:15); God "refused the tabernacle of Joseph" (78:67); "thou that leadest Joseph like a flock" (80:1); "ordained in Joseph for a testimony" (81:5) — the Joseph name in the Psalter. The connection object spans Ps 77:15–81:5; the exact verses are Ps 77:15, 78:67, 80:1, and 81:5.
The Joseph psalm: feet in shackles, neck in irons; the king made him master of his household (BiblicalTraining).

Daniel's understanding in visions and dreams; Nebuchadnezzar's dreams — the later dream-interpretation parallel to Joseph (BDB's ḥălôm range includes Daniel). The connection object spans Dan 1:17–2:3; the exact verses are Dan 1:17 and 2:1–3.
The two sticks: Judah and Joseph — the divided kingdom figured by the two names.
Joseph receives two portions — the double-portion fulfilment (BiblicalTraining).
"The house of Joseph" — the northern kingdom. The connection object spans Amos 5:6–6:6; the exact verses are Amos 5:6, 5:15, and 6:6.
"The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame".
"I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph".
"There arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph" — the hinge into the Exodus era (BiblicalTraining).
The 430 years — the dating anchor.
Moses takes Joseph's bones up out of Egypt — the oath kept.
The 480 years — the dating anchor.
"Out of Egypt have I called my son" (Hos 11:1) — the Exodus guidance K&D contrast with the Joseph typology.
Stephen's retelling: jealousy, God with Joseph, wisdom before Pharaoh, the pattern of Israel rejecting deliverers (BiblicalTraining).
"By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel; and gave commandment concerning his bones".
The tribe of Joseph alongside Manasseh in the sealing (BiblicalTraining).
